title: Kidney Stones: Urology Referral and Prevention

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult in primary care, the emergency department or a urology clinic in Saudi Arabia with suspected or confirmed renal or ureteric stones: imaging and tests, pain and nausea control, medical expulsive therapy, recognition of the obstructed infected kidney, urology referral and prevention of recurrence, using the Saudi Urolithiasis Guidelines (Saudi Urological Association, 2024) and NICE NG118, with doses, dilution, administration and contraindications taken from product labels. Non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) is the reference imaging test.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-20.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi Ministry of Health kidney stone protocol was opened; the Saudi source is the Saudi Urological Association (SUA) 2024 guideline, so the authority is shown as Other.

SUA 2024 names the drug classes for pain relief, medical expulsive therapy, antibiotics and prevention but gives no doses (its pain-relief figure could not be read from the open-access text); every dose, dilution and administration step comes from the product label named in each row.

Several drugs are used outside their labelled indication in stone disease: tamsulosin (NICE NG118 Recommendation 1.3.1 records it as off-label), ondansetron for colic nausea, potassium citrate for uric acid chemolysis dosing to a urine pH target (SUA Recommendation 10 sets pH 7.0 to 7.2), and the US piperacillin-tazobactam and meropenem labels do not list urinary tract infection as an indication. Confirm against the local formulary.

The US piperacillin-tazobactam label gives 3.375 g every 6 hours as the usual adult dose; some units use 4.5 g for sepsis, which this topic does not state because the sources opened do not give it for a urinary source.
SUA 2024 lists imipenem as a third carbapenem option for the obstructed infected kidney; imipenem is not written as a regimen here because its label was not opened.
Diclofenac comes from a United Kingdom Summary of Product Characteristics because the US injection is not marketed; the Saudi product label was not checked.
Thiazide for hypercalciuria and febuxostat as second-line for hyperuricosuria are named in SUA 2024 Section 4 but no regimen is written because no dose was found in the sources opened.
Safe analgesia in pregnancy beyond avoiding NSAIDs (for example paracetamol first) is not stated in SUA 2024 as opened; confirm with the obstetric team.
No antibiotic regimen is given for severe beta-lactam allergy; follow local microbiology advice.
Allopurinol: the US label advises considering HLA-B*58:01 testing where the allele is common; Saudi allele frequency was not checked.
Differentials are standard clinical knowledge and are not drawn from one source section.

Figures were read through automated extraction of the open-access journal XML, NICE web text, the electronic Medicines Compendium and DailyMed label XML; spot-check each dose against the source during clinical review.
Paediatric stone management, percutaneous nephrolithotomy technique and cystine stone drug regimens are outside this primary-care and referral topic.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register returned an empty page from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before ordering.

pathophysiology.summary: Stones form when urine is supersaturated with stone-forming salts and low in inhibitors such as citrate and water volume. Around 85% of kidney stones in the Saudi population are calcium oxalate (SUA 2024, Section 1 Introduction). Saudi Arabia has a high burden: SUA 2024 quotes a prevalence of 6.2% to 11.2%, a 2.5-fold higher risk than other populations, and rising over time; hot climate, low fluid intake, diet and obesity are likely drivers (SUA 2024, Section 1 Introduction). Pain comes from sudden stretching of the ureter or renal capsule when a stone blocks urine flow; it is felt as loin pain moving to the groin with vomiting (SUA 2024, Section 1; NICE NG118 Recommendation 1.2). A stone that blocks the kidney while the urine behind it is infected can cause bacteria to enter the bloodstream; this is a surgical emergency that needs drainage as well as antibiotics (SUA 2024, Recommendation 24 and 25). Stone type decides prevention: uric acid stones form in acid urine (pH below 5.5) and are not seen on plain X-ray; cystine stones come from an inherited transport defect; struvite stones follow urea-splitting infection (SUA 2024, Section 4). A stone of 5 mm or less usually passes, while 10 mm or more rarely does; stones that grow by more than 3 mm, cause infection or obstruct need intervention (SUA 2024, Recommendation 11 to 13).

symptoms: Sudden severe loin pain that comes in waves and may spread to the groin or genitals, with restlessness, nausea and vomiting (SUA 2024, Section 1).
Blood in the urine, urgency, frequency or burning when passing urine as the stone nears the bladder (SUA 2024, Section 1).
Some stones cause no symptoms and are found by chance on scans (SUA 2024, Section 1 Introduction).
Fever, rigors and feeling very unwell with flank pain suggest an infected blocked kidney (SUA 2024, Recommendation 24).
physicalSigns: Loin or flank tenderness; the patient cannot lie still.
Fever, fast heart rate, low blood pressure or confusion in the infected blocked kidney (SUA 2024, Recommendation 24).
Blood on urine dipstick; leukocytes and nitrites if infection is present (SUA 2024, Section 1, Urine).
redFlags: Fever with flank pain or a blocked kidney: urgent decompression by stent or nephrostomy and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics; delay definitive stone surgery until sepsis has cleared (SUA 2024, Recommendation 24 and 25).
Solitary kidney, kidney transplant or known renal impairment with an obstructing stone: urgent urology review (SUA 2024, Section 3 indications for intervention).
Pain not controlled by the analgesia ladder, or persistent vomiting: admit for intravenous drugs and imaging (NICE NG118, Recommendation 1.2).
Pregnant woman with renal colic: ultrasound first, observe, avoid NSAIDs, involve obstetrics and urology (SUA 2024, Recommendation 4 and Recommendation 32 and 33).
Suspected aortic or gynaecological emergency in an older patient or woman of childbearing age: do not assume stone; image early (clinical judgment).
Acute kidney injury or anuria: urgent decompression and nephrology involvement (SUA 2024, Section 3 indications for intervention).
precipitants: Low fluid intake, hot climate and sweating; high salt, animal protein and oxalate intake (SUA 2024, Section 4).
Previous stones, family history, obesity and diabetes (SUA 2024, Section 1 Introduction).
Urinary infection, urinary diversion, bowel resection, bariatric surgery or inflammatory bowel disease (SUA 2024, Section 3 and Recommendation 42).
Hyperparathyroidism, renal tubular acidosis, cystinuria and high urinary uric acid (SUA 2024, Section 4).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fever, urinary symptoms and loin tenderness; imaging shows no obstructing stone; a stone with infection above it needs urgent drainage (SUA 2024, Recommendation 24).
Right upper abdominal pain after fatty food with a positive Murphy sign; ultrasound shows gallstones and urine is usually clean (clinical judgment).
Pain moves to one iliac fossa with guarding and raised inflammatory markers; non-contrast imaging shows the inflamed bowel (clinical judgment).
Woman of childbearing age with pelvic pain and a positive pregnancy test or adnexal mass; always test pregnancy before imaging (SUA 2024, Recommendation 4; clinical judgment).

differentials.condition: Ruptured or leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Older patient with vascular disease, hypotension and a pulsatile mass; needs immediate imaging, not analgesia alone (clinical judgment).

differentials.condition: Testicular torsion or musculoskeletal back pain
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Torsion: acutely tender high testis; musculoskeletal pain changes with movement and the urine is normal (clinical judgment).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess and image
actions: Take a pain, urinary and past stone history and look for fever, shock, solitary kidney, pregnancy or kidney injury (SUA 2024, Section 1).
Test urine by dipstick, send culture if infection is suspected, and send blood tests including full blood count, creatinine, electrolytes, calcium and uric acid (SUA 2024, Section 1).

Image with non-contrast computed tomography; low-dose protocol if body mass index is below 30; use ultrasound with or without plain film where scanning is unavailable, in pregnancy and in children (SUA 2024, Recommendation 1 to 4).
Pregnancy test in women of childbearing age before any scan or drug.

clinicalManagement.title: Control pain and nausea
actions: Offer a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) by any route first (NICE NG118 Recommendation 1.2.1).
If NSAIDs are contraindicated or not enough, give intravenous paracetamol; use opioids only if both fail (NICE NG118 Recommendation 1.2.2 and 1.2.3).
Do not give antispasmodics (NICE NG118 Recommendation 1.2.4).
Treat vomiting with an antiemetic and correct dehydration before NSAIDs if the patient is volume depleted (ketorolac label).
Pregnancy: avoid NSAIDs and observe; involve obstetrics (SUA 2024, Recommendation 32 and 33).

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise the obstructed infected kidney
actions: Fever or sepsis with an obstructing stone is an emergency: start intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and arrange urgent decompression with a ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy (SUA 2024, Recommendation 24 and 25).
Send culture at decompression; delay definitive stone treatment until the infection has cleared (SUA 2024, Recommendation 24).
Step down antibiotics 48 hours after fever settles according to culture; plan 10 to 14 days in total (SUA 2024, Recommendation 25).

clinicalManagement.title: Decide: wait for passage or refer
actions: Ureteric stone under 10 mm with controlled pain and no infection, obstruction or kidney injury: offer an alpha-blocker for a distal stone (SUA 2024, Recommendation 9; NICE NG118 Recommendation 1.3.1); the sources do not set a maximum duration.
Refer to urology within a few days for stones above 10 mm, stones with growth, ongoing pain, solitary kidney, kidney injury or any infection (SUA 2024, Section 3).
Asymptomatic stone: observe 5 mm or less; image at 6 months then yearly; intervene if growth exceeds 3 mm or stone exceeds 15 mm (SUA 2024, Recommendation 11 to 13).
Ask the patient to strain urine and bring any passed stone for analysis (SUA 2024, Recommendation 8).
Warn the patient to return at once with fever, uncontrolled pain, vomiting or no urine.

clinicalManagement.title: Prevent the next stone
actions: Advise urine output of 2.0 to 2.5 L a day (drink 2.5 to 3.0 L), calcium 1 to 1.2 g a day, sodium chloride 4 to 5 g a day and animal protein 0.8 to 1.0 g per kg a day (SUA 2024, Recommendation 40 and 41).

Send stone analysis; order a full metabolic evaluation with 24-hour urine for frequent recurrence, children, brushite, solitary kidney, renal impairment, bowel resection, bariatric surgery or inflammatory bowel disease (SUA 2024, Recommendation 42).
Add serum calcium and parathyroid hormone if calcium is high or high-normal (SUA 2024, Section 4).
Match drug to cause: alkaline citrate for low urinary citrate or uric acid stones; allopurinol for high urinary uric acid; thiazide (specialist) for high urinary calcium (SUA 2024, Section 4).
Uric acid stones: suspect if urine pH is below 5.5 and the stone is radiolucent; oral chemolysis aims at urine pH 7.0 to 7.2 (SUA 2024, Recommendation 10).

regimens.indication: Acute renal colic: first-line pain relief
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with renal colic and no NSAID contraindication
regimens.dose: 75 mg (one 3 mL ampoule) as a single dose; a second 75 mg ampoule 30 minutes later if needed; maximum 150 mg in 24 hours. Dilution and preparation: none; give as supplied.
regimens.route: Deep intramuscular injection into the upper outer quadrant of the buttock; use the other buttock for a second injection; never as an intravenous bolus (Voltarol ampoule SmPC, Section 4.2)
regimens.frequency: Once; repeat once after 30 minutes if pain persists
regimens.duration: No more than 2 days, then change to an oral drug
adjustments: Elderly and frail or low-weight patients: use the lowest effective dose (SmPC, Section 4.2).
Renal: contraindicated in renal failure; caution in mild to moderate impairment (SmPC, Section 4.2).
Hepatic: contraindicated in hepatic failure (SmPC, Section 4.2).

Pregnancy: SUA 2024 Recommendation 32 and 33 advise observation and general avoidance of NSAIDs in pregnancy; shock-wave lithotripsy is contraindicated and the second trimester is the safest time for ureteroscopy.
Last trimester of pregnancy: contraindicated (SmPC, Section 4.3).

Product contains sodium metabisulphite and benzyl alcohol (SmPC, Section 6.1).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register returned an empty page from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before ordering.
monitoring: Pain score at 30 minutes; creatinine if the patient is old, dehydrated or on a diuretic or renin-angiotensin drug (SmPC, Section 4.4).
Gastrointestinal bleeding and cardiovascular events with repeated use.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to diclofenac or sodium metabisulphite; asthma, angioedema, urticaria or rhinitis triggered by aspirin or another NSAID (SmPC, Section 4.3).
Active or past gastrointestinal ulcer, bleeding or perforation (SmPC, Section 4.3).
Hepatic failure, renal failure, established heart failure (NYHA II to IV), ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease (SmPC, Section 4.3).
Last trimester of pregnancy (SmPC, Section 4.3).
Check for NSAID-sensitive asthma, angioedema or urticaria before the first dose.

regimens.frequency: Single dose; repeat every 6 hours if required
regimens.duration: Maximum 5 days in total by any route
adjustments: Correct hypovolaemia before giving (ketorolac label).
Elderly, renal impairment or under 50 kg: use the lower dose (ketorolac label).

Labour and delivery: contraindicated; Pregnancy: SUA 2024 Recommendation 32 and 33 advise observation and general avoidance of NSAIDs in pregnancy; shock-wave lithotripsy is contraindicated and the second trimester is the safest time for ureteroscopy.

regimens.indication: Renal colic when NSAIDs are contraindicated or do not give enough pain relief
regimens.dose: 1,000 mg (100 mL ready-to-use solution) for adults of 50 kg or more; 15 mg/kg for adults under 50 kg; minimum 4 hours between doses; maximum single dose 1,000 mg; maximum 4,000 mg a day from all sources (75 mg/kg a day under 50 kg). adjustments: Count all paracetamol from other products in the 4 g daily limit (Ofirmev label, Section 2.1).
Severe hepatic impairment: contraindicated; caution with alcohol use and low body weight (Ofirmev label).

adjustments: Creatinine clearance 20 to 40 mL/min: 2.25 g every 6 hours; below 20 mL/min: 2.25 g every 8 hours; haemodialysis or continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis: 2.25 g every 12 hours (label, Section 2.3).
Check local policy before using a higher dose for sepsis.

regimens.indication: Low urinary citrate, renal tubular acidosis with calcium stones, or uric acid stones
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with recurrent stones and low citrate or uric acid stones
regimens.dose: Urinary citrate below 150 mg a day: 60 mEq a day (30 mEq twice daily or 20 mEq three times daily); urinary citrate above 150 mg a day: 30 mEq a day (15 mEq twice daily or 10 mEq three times daily); do not exceed 100 mEq a day. Dilution and preparation: none; extended-release tablets of 10 mEq or 15 mEq.
regimens.route: Oral; with meals or within 30 minutes after a meal or bedtime snack; swallow whole with water (Urocit-K label, Section 2.2 and Section 2.3)
regimens.duration: Long-term; adjust to 24-hour urinary citrate and pH (target pH 6.0 to 7.0; uric acid chemolysis 7.0 to 7.2 in SUA 2024 Recommendation 10)
adjustments: Renal: contraindicated in significant renal insufficiency (glomerular filtration rate below 0.7 mL/kg/min).
Uric acid stones: SUA 2024 Recommendation 10 supports oral chemolysis to urine pH 7.0 to 7.2; the label dosing is to urine pH 6.0 to 7.0.
Take with plenty of fluid and a low-salt diet; keep urine volume at least 2 L a day (label, Section 2.1).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register returned an empty page from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before ordering.
monitoring: Serum sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, creatinine and full blood count every 4 months, more often with cardiac or renal disease; periodic electrocardiogram (label, Section 2.1).
24-hour urine citrate and urine pH to judge dose; stop if potassium rises, creatinine rises or haemoglobin falls (label, Section 2.1).
contraindications: Hyperkalaemia or conditions that predispose to it, such as chronic renal failure, uncontrolled diabetes, dehydration, adrenal insufficiency or potassium-sparing diuretics (Urocit-K label, Section 4).
Delayed tablet passage through the gut, such as delayed gastric emptying, oesophageal compression, intestinal obstruction or anticholinergic use (label, Section 4).
Peptic ulcer disease; active urinary tract infection (label, Section 4).
Renal insufficiency (glomerular filtration rate below 0.7 mL/kg/min) (label, Section 4).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Non-contrast computed tomography of abdomen and pelvis (SUA 2024, Recommendation 1); low-dose protocol if body mass index is below 30 (Recommendation 2); ultrasound with or without plain film if scanning is unavailable (Recommendation 3); ultrasound first in pregnancy and children (Recommendation 4).
Ureteric stone under 10 mm; distal stones above 5 mm and below 10 mm benefit from an alpha-blocker (SUA 2024, Recommendation 9; NICE NG118 Recommendation 1.3.1).

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Asymptomatic kidney stone: size and surveillance
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: 5 mm or less likely to pass; 10 mm or more unlikely to pass; image at 6 months then yearly; intervene if growth exceeds 3 mm (SUA 2024, Recommendation 11 to 13).
Stone above 15 mm, infection, obstruction, growth, pain or patient choice (SUA 2024, Section 3 indications of surgical intervention).

Obstructing stone with fever or systemic infection: decompress urgently, culture at decompression, broad-spectrum antibiotics; step down after 48 hours without fever; 10 to 14 days in total (SUA 2024, Recommendation 24 and 25).
Frequent recurrence, children, brushite stones, solitary kidney, renal impairment, bowel resection or bariatric surgery, inflammatory bowel disease (SUA 2024, Recommendation 42).
Urine volume 2.0 to 2.5 L a day (fluid 2.5 to 3.0 L); calcium 1 to 1.2 g a day; sodium chloride 4 to 5 g a day; animal protein 0.8 to 1.0 g per kg a day (SUA 2024, Recommendation 40 and 41).

teaching.scope: Adult in primary care, the emergency department or a urology clinic in Saudi Arabia with suspected or confirmed renal or ureteric stones: imaging and tests, pain and nausea control, medical expulsive therapy, recognition of the obstructed infected kidney, urology referral and prevention of recurrence, using the Saudi Urolithiasis Guidelines (Saudi Urological Association, 2024) and NICE NG118, with doses, dilution, administration and contraindications taken from product labels. Non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) is the reference imaging test.
learningObjectives: Image suspected renal colic with non-contrast computed tomography, or ultrasound in pregnancy and children.
Control pain in steps: NSAID, intravenous paracetamol, then opioid; avoid antispasmodics.
Recognise the infected blocked kidney and arrange urgent decompression with antibiotics.
Choose prevention by stone type, fluids and diet, with 24-hour urine tests for high-risk patients.
pitfalls: Giving an NSAID to a dehydrated patient without fluids, risking kidney injury.
Treating a febrile patient with a stone as simple colic and discharging.
Using antispasmodics, which NICE says not to offer.
Skipping pregnancy testing before imaging or drugs.
Starting potassium citrate before checking potassium, creatinine and urine infection.
keyPoints: Fever with a stone is an emergency: drain the kidney before any definitive stone surgery.
A passed stone must be sent for analysis because the type decides prevention.
NSAIDs are contraindicated in renal failure, ulcer disease, heart disease, late pregnancy and NSAID-sensitive asthma.
Alpha-blockers are used off-label for distal stones under 10 mm and do not replace imaging follow-up.
Potassium citrate is dangerous with high potassium or poor kidney function.

patientEducation: Drink enough fluid to pass 2 to 2.5 litres of urine a day, spread across the day, more in hot weather.
Return at once with fever, shaking chills, vomiting that stops you drinking, severe pain not helped by tablets, or passing no urine.
Strain your urine and bring any stone you pass to the clinic; it tells us how to prevent the next one.
Take painkillers and tamsulosin as written; do not take other anti-inflammatory tablets with them.
Potassium citrate must be swallowed whole with meals and needs regular blood tests.
lifestyleAndDiet: Keep calcium normal at 1 to 1.2 g a day from food such as dairy; do not cut calcium.
Limit salt to 4 to 5 g a day and animal protein to 0.8 to 1.0 g per kg a day.
Eat plenty of vegetables and fibre; reduce high-oxalate foods and purines if advised.
mdtReferrals: Primary care physician; emergency physician; urologist; interventional radiologist (nephrostomy); nephrologist for recurrent stones or kidney impairment; clinical pharmacist; dietitian; obstetrician for pregnancy.
dischargeCriteria: Pain controlled with oral drugs; no fever, vomiting or kidney injury; stone size and position known; urology referral booked if stone is above 10 mm, growing or persistent; written safety-net advice and stone strainer given.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Repeat imaging to confirm passage or growth (surveillance at 6 months then yearly for untreated stones); urology follow-up as arranged; stone analysis result reviewed; 24-hour urine results used to start citrate or allopurinol; review dietary targets and urine volume yearly.
